chunks: I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) about a man who said to another man: 'Write, O so-and-so, to my wife regarding her divorce,' or 'Write to my slave regarding his emancipation' — does that constitute a divorce or an emancipation?

He said: Neither a divorce nor an emancipation comes into effect until he utters it with his tongue or writes it with his own hand, while intending the divorce or the emancipation, and this must be done by him in accordance with (the counting of) the new moons and with witnesses, and he must be absent from his wife.

key_terms.الأهلة: New moons — reference to the lunar months counted in the waiting period (iddah)
key_terms.خط بيده: Writing with his own hand — the alternative mode of effecting talaq or itq
key_terms.شهود: Witnesses — required observers for the validity of the divorce
key_terms.طلاق: Divorce (talaq) — the formal dissolution of marriage by the husband's declaration
key_terms.عتق: Emancipation (itq) — the formal freeing of a slave by the master's declaration
key_terms.لسان: Tongue — the requirement of verbal utterance for legal effect

ai.seo_question: Does delegating someone else to write a divorce or emancipation letter make it valid in Shia Islamic law?
ai.summary: Imam al-Baqir (peace be upon him) rules that delegating to another person the mere act of writing a divorce or emancipation letter, without the husband or master himself speaking or writing the formula with his own hand and intent, is legally ineffective. The ruling specifies three additional conditions for a valid divorce of an absent wife: the husband must personally pronounce or write the formula with intent, the lunar-month waiting period must be observed, and witnesses must be present. This reflects the Shia jurisprudential emphasis on direct personal agency (mubashara) and intention (niyya) as conditions for the validity of major legal acts.
